concepts.definition: A recorded event or measurement, distinct from an explanation of why it occurred.
A candidate explanation whose predictions can be compared with evidence.

chapters.title: Observation and explanation
chapters.summary: An observed result can support several explanations. Their different predictions guide further inquiry.

blocks.title: What was observed and what is inferred
blocks.text:
You walk outside and see wet pavement. The observation describes the visible condition. Rain is one hypothesis about its cause, but a sprinkler or street cleaner could produce that condition too.

An explanation being compatible with the observation does not establish it as the actual cause. Separating the result from its possible causes keeps a plausible interpretation from silently becoming a recorded fact.

blocks.title: Different predictions identify useful evidence
blocks.text:
The next question is what else each hypothesis predicts. Rain may wet exposed areas beyond this pavement; a sprinkler may leave a localized pattern near the watered area. Looking at those patterns can help distinguish the two explanations.

The comparison is only as useful as its assumptions. An earlier shower may have dried unevenly, and a sprinkler may operate while it rains. A result can weaken a candidate explanation without proving its rival. The goal is to seek discriminating evidence, not merely collect facts compatible with a preferred story.

blocks.title: From an observed result to a useful comparison
blocks.caption: Original static schematic. The arrows indicate reasoning roles, not proof that a particular cause occurred.
blocks.alternative: Wet pavement is the observation. It supports candidate hypotheses such as rain or a sprinkler. Compare their predicted wetness patterns in nearby areas. The result may discriminate among candidates, but it does not automatically prove one.

steps.title: Reasoning roles
steps.explanation: An observation prompts candidate explanations; their predictions guide a comparison. Compatibility is not proof.

blocks.title: What this lesson adds
blocks.text: Keep the observation, candidate explanation, and predicted evidence separate. A useful next observation distinguishes alternatives; finding support for one explanation does not make every other explanation impossible.

outcomes.text: Explain the difference between a recorded observation and a candidate explanation, and why comparing predictions is useful.

weeks.title: Observation and explanation
weeks.notes:
This illustrative grouping connects two ideas: what we observe and what might explain it. The lesson uses wet pavement to show why an explanation needs more than compatibility with one result.

The connection is inference: distinguish the result from candidate causes, then compare what those causes predict. The diagram makes those roles visible without replacing the explanation.
